name: Portland Streets Then and Now: Liveliness and Virtual Audit
description:
Method replication: participants see 20 Portland street views in random order, some from 2007–2009 and some from 2015–2018, and for each one rate liveliness on five levels (Lively to Deserted) and fill in the paper's virtual audit checklist (pedestrians, cyclists, dogs, sidewalks, crosswalks, bike signs, surface problems, street trees, buildings of three or more storeys, sidewalk signs, construction, graffiti, large parking lots, weather); the images are not the paper's stimuli (40 newly fetched Google Street View locations across Portland, each captured once in 2007–2009 and once in 2015–2018 facing the same direction, 80 images). Answers are stored as the position of the chosen category, starting at 0 (for liveliness 0 = Lively, 4 = Deserted).

Original study: Hanibuchi, Nagata, Banis, Shobe & Nakaya (2024), The Professional Geographer 76(2), 180–193. Up to 25 intersections were sampled in each of Portland's 142 census tracts (3,508 intersections) where Street View Time Machine had images from both 2007–2009 and 2015–2018, giving 24,242 images, one per street direction per period. Eleven untrained crowd workers from the Japanese platform Lancers, each covering whole tracts with images in random order, filled in the checklist and the liveliness rating; agreement was tested against a gold standard. The city became livelier, linked to more pedestrians and cyclists.

Differences from the original study: (1) random street points, not only intersections; (2) the paper's liveliness scale names only the ends and the middle, so "Fairly lively" and "Fairly deserted" are written for this template; (3) participants rate a random 20 images instead of all images of their assigned tracts, so one person may not see both periods of the same place; (4) no reliability test against a gold standard.
author: Hanibuchi, Nagata, Banis, Shobe & Nakaya

dimensions.label: Liveliness: which is closer to your impression?
Pedestrians: people walking (not sitting or in vehicles)
Cyclists (riding or walking a bike; not parked bikes)
Sidewalks physically separated from the road
Bike lane sign (symbol or text) painted on the street
Holes, steps or cracks on the street surface
Street trees (including garden trees, trees without leaves; not distant hills)
Buildings of three storeys or more (not bridges or towers)
Shop frame signs placed on the sidewalk
Graffiti on walls, doors or street (not murals)
Parking lot with space for 10 or more cars (not street parking)
